title: Society for Marketers (non-profit): changing the fiscal year to the calendar year, accounting cycle, reporting timeline and annual report
participant_role: Executive director of the Society for Marketers, a 501(c)(3) membership association, proposing an accounting plan
judge_role: President of the board of directors of the Society for Marketers
scenario:
You are to assume the role of executive director of the SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS, a non-profit, 501(c)3 membership association that serves marketing professionals. The president of the board of directors (judge) has asked for your help in developing an accounting plan to review and propose standard operating procedures around its finance functions.

SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS has existed for the past 40 years, but within the past five years has had to change its core mission, membership model, and programs and services offered to meet the changing needs of their professional members. For example, the annual conference which used to host 15,000 attendees was on a gradual decline, but surveys indicated that attendees and members who were not attending the conference would prefer the meeting be moved from April to October. As a result of moving the conference to October three years ago, attendance has been on the rise with a record attendance of 18,000 last year. The conference accounts for nearly 60% of the accounting transactions within the budget of the SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS.

Currently, the fiscal year for the SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS begins July 1 and ends June 30. Non-profits have a luxury that most individuals and corporate businesses do not: they can select their fiscal year-end for IRS purposes. Membership dues used to run the fiscal year, but now, based on feedback from potential and current members, membership now runs one full year starting with the month the member joins. Most corporate partners of the SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS operate their fiscal year on the calendar year (January 1 to December 31).

The president of the board of directors of SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS (judge) wants you to help create an accounting plan to review and propose standard operating procedures around its finance functions. Specifically, the president of the board of directors (judge) wants you to discuss the following:
- A rationale for adjusting the fiscal year to match the calendar year.
- Impacts to the accounting cycle when the fiscal year is adjusted.
- A proposed timeline for reporting, including the audit, to the board of directors.
- Financial documents that should be included in the annual report.
- Why financial information is imperative to the operations of the association.

You will present your accounting plan to the president of the board of directors (judge) in a role-play to take place in the president's (judge's) office. The president of the board of directors (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the plan and have answered the president's (judge's) questions, the president (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer argues that a calendar fiscal year fits the October conference, the rolling membership model and corporate partners' reporting, explains that the transition year will be a short accounting cycle, proposes quarterly board reports, an annual audit and Form 990 filing as governance practices, lists the audit, statement of financial position, statement of activities and income and expense charts for the annual report, and explains that financial information drives decisions, mission alignment and the board's fiduciary duties.

by_task.task: Rationale for a calendar fiscal year
answer: The October conference, nearly 60% of transactions, can be fully closed out by December 31 so the whole event lands in one fiscal year
Membership dues no longer run July to June, so there is no reason to keep the fiscal year tied to them
A calendar year matches most corporate partners' fiscal years, which helps with sponsorships, funding and comparable reporting
As a non-profit, the Society is free to choose its year-end for IRS purposes

The accounting cycle is the process of recording and processing transactions from when they occur until they appear in the financial statements: journalize, post, trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, close
The transition year runs July 1 to December 31, so that year's cycle is only six months (a short year)
Closing entries, adjusting entries and the audit all move to a December 31 year-end
Budgets must be rebuilt for the short year and then for the new January to December year
Quarterly financial reports to the board of directors (budget vs. actual)
Annual independent audit soon after the December 31 year-end
File Form 990 with the IRS after the audit is complete
Present the audited statements and annual report to the board and members; these practices are components of a well-governed organization
Full copy of the completed audit
Statement of Financial Position (non-profit balance sheet)
Statement of Activities (non-profit income statement)
Pie charts of major sources of income and major categories of expenses
Members, major donors and funders use this information
Needed to make sound business decisions such as pricing the conference and dues
Aligns programs and services with the mission by showing what each costs and earns
Lets the board carry out its governance and fiduciary duties (transparency, audit oversight)
Funders, partners and members expect accurate, timely reporting

judge_question_answers.question: How do we change our year-end with the IRS?
answer: Prepare the next Form 990 using the new December 31 year-end
That return will cover a short year (July 1 to December 31) because the IRS does not allow a return to cover more than 12 months

judge_question_answers.question: Are there any other considerations we may need to contemplate when changing our year-end?
answer: Review the organization's governing documents (bylaws, policies) to make sure they allow the change and stay in compliance
Financial comparisons will be less useful during the transition because the short year covers less than 12 months
Plan the budget and cash flow carefully for the short year

key_concepts.definition: The 12-month period a business uses for accounting and tax reporting. It does not have to match the calendar year, and non-profits can choose their year-end for IRS purposes.
An accounting period shorter than 12 months created when an organization changes its fiscal year-end; the IRS requires a separate return for it.
The steps from recording a transaction to reporting it in the financial statements: journalize, post, prepare a trial balance, adjust, prepare statements and close the books.
The annual information return a tax-exempt non-profit files with the IRS, reporting its finances, programs and governance.
The non-profit version of a balance sheet, showing assets, liabilities and net assets at a point in time.
The non-profit version of an income statement, showing revenues, expenses and the change in net assets for a period.
A yearly publication to members, donors and funders that includes audited financial statements and summaries of income sources and expense categories.
An examination of the financial statements by an outside CPA firm that gives assurance they are fairly presented.
The board's legal responsibility to oversee the organization's finances carefully, honestly and in the interest of the organization.
One with regular financial reporting to the board, an annual audit, timely tax filings, clear policies and transparency to stakeholders.
Using a budget to plan revenues and expenses and comparing budget to actual results each quarter to control spending and guide decisions.

notes: The PDF SOLUTION section says answers will vary and gives suggested points for each task and both judge questions; the JSON follows those points with modest elaboration (for example the six-month length of the short year and budgeting for it, which the PDF implies but does not state).
